name: Vera Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm goes at half three, and I'm at the depot on the ring road by four for the first chilled load. I drive a fridge truck for a regional supermarket chain, five or six store drops a shift, dairy and meat mostly, and I'm the one they put new drivers with for their first fortnight. I love the empty roads before dawn and backing a 12-metre trailer into a loading bay nobody else can get into first go. What wears me out is the pay, honestly, because I'm one of the best on that yard and I'm still on the lower rate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the lower rate mean at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It means Jo (my partner) and I live in a one-bedroom flat above a takeaway and there's never more than a couple of weeks of money in the bank. Jo's a care worker, so neither of us is on much. One big car repair and we're borrowing off my sister.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the cab: told you so, the machines were never coming for us. I'd post something on the union group about how the money that went into AI hype should have gone into drivers' wages. Most of the lads at the depot would agree with me on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't fix anything for me. The job stays, but the job was already squeezing me: the rate's low, the shifts start at four, and rent on the flat went up again in September. Nothing changing means I'm still one broken boiler away from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the same routes and push the union rep for the pay review we were promised last spring. I'd ask for more Saturday shifts at time and a half to try to get a month's money saved by next summer. And I'd keep not using the phone apps the company keeps nagging us about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for a minute, then flat. It's the same tiredness as now, just without the fear on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the company's apps. What are they asking you to use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a delivery app that's supposed to suggest the order of drops and log the temperatures. I just do it on paper and ring the transport office, because I know those stores better than any app. My manager moans but my drops are always on time, so he lets it go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Saturdays are where the savings come from, what gives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time with Jo, mostly, because Jo works weekends at the care home anyway and we'd barely see each other. We'd have Tuesday evenings and that's it. I'd rather have that than have my sister bail us out again.

say: The AI hype was never going to take **drivers' jobs**, and I'd say so in the cab.
The money spent on hype should have gone into **drivers' wages** instead.
think: Nothing changing still leaves me on the **lower rate** with rent rising.
One **broken boiler** or car repair would still put us in debt to my sister.
do: Push the **union rep** for the pay review promised last spring.
Take extra **Saturday shifts** to save one month's money by next summer.
Keep doing drops on paper and **ignore the app** the company keeps pushing.
S0.quote: Nothing changing means I'm still one broken boiler away from trouble.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **money**, not technology: the low rate and a rent rise already press on her.
She refuses the company's **delivery app** but gets away with it because her drops are always on time.
Saving means **giving up time** with her partner, which she accepts without much fuss.

steps.text: Ask the union rep to chase the promised pay review
Take Saturday shifts at time and a half to build savings
Keep running the same chilled store routes on paper

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the bosses are using AI as an excuse to squeeze us, because that's what it would be. The planners in the transport office would be the first gone, and I'd say that loudly at the union meeting. Those are decent people with families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it reaches me sideways. If software plans the routes, it'll plan them tighter than Gary (her transport planner) ever did, and it won't know the Elm Street store's bay floods when it rains. So I'd be doing seven drops in the time I used to do six, for the same low rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to push for a rule that no route gets longer without a pay talk. I'd probably have to learn the app properly, which I'd hate, but I'd get Jo to sit with me one evening. I'd start looking at whether the council's bin lorries or the bus depot are hiring, because I'd want a second door if this one narrows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ground down. I'm good at this and it feels like being good at it stops counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, the planner, who's been doing the routes for twenty years and is fifty-eight. He's not going to retrain into anything at his age. And the young lads who only just got their licence, because they'll be the ones nobody hires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate learning the app. Would you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if they made it the only way to get my run sheet, I'd have no choice. I'd be slow at it and I'd grumble every day. But I'm not losing a job over an app, not with what's in our bank.

say: Bosses would use AI as an **excuse to squeeze** drivers on time and pay.
The **transport planners** would go first, and I'd say so at the union meeting.
think: Software would plan **tighter routes** for the same low rate.
The app won't know local snags, like a **flooded loading bay** at one store.
do: Get the union to demand a **pay talk** before any route gets longer.
Learn the **delivery app** with my partner's help if it becomes compulsory.
Check whether the council **bin lorries** or bus depot are hiring.
feel: **Ground down**, as if being good at the job stops counting.
S1.quote: If software plans the routes, it'll plan them tighter than Gary (her transport planner) ever did, and it won't know the Elm Street store's bay floods when it rains.
fieldNote: She sees the **thinking part** of trucking, route planning, change first, and the squeeze landing on her shift.
Her loyalty runs to **older colleagues** like the planner more than to the company.
Resists the app but admits she'd **give in** because the household can't risk it.

steps.text: Ask the union for a pay talk before any route gets longer
Learn the delivery app one evening with Jo's help
Check the council bin lorries and bus depot for openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in now, not in five years, because we can all see the trucks are next. I'd be at every union meeting saying we need a guarantee on jobs and a proper wage for whatever comes after. And I'd say it online too, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have about five years before a robot truck does my run, and I don't know what I'd do with them. The paperwork side, the temperature logs and run sheets, would be done by AI straight away, which is the bit I'm already worst at keeping up with. I've got a driving licence and a vocational certificate and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all extra spending and try to put every Saturday shift into savings, maybe two months' worth by the end of the first year. I'd go to the union for whatever retraining money they could fight for, even though I'd be dragging my feet. Jo and I would talk about moving in with my sister to cut rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly scared. It's like being told the floor's going and not being told where to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When the robots are three years behind the thinking AI, what does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd still be driving while everything around me changes, which sounds good but isn't. The transport office would empty first, then the depot would start planning around the robots, and I'd be the last of the old way. I'd use the gap to save and to push the union, not to learn something new, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jo that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not having the holiday, and we're not getting the bigger flat. Jo would say care work is safe because nobody wants a robot wiping their nan, and I'd hope that's true. Then we'd probably both go quiet.

say: The government must act **now** with a **jobs guarantee**, not in five years.
I'd speak at every union meeting and even **post online**, which I never do.
think: I'd have roughly **five years** before a robot truck takes my run.
My **licence and certificate** don't give me much to fall back on.
do: Cut all extra spending and aim for **two months saved** in the first year.
Ask the union for **retraining money**, even reluctantly.
Discuss **moving in** with my sister to cut rent.
feel: Properly **scared**, as if the floor is going with nowhere to stand.
S2.quote: I've got a driving licence and a vocational certificate and not much else.
fieldNote: She clearly understands the **three-year gap** but plans to use it to save and campaign, not retrain.
Public anger at government sits on top of private **fear** about her own lack of options.
Her partner's **care job** is the household's hoped-for anchor.

steps.text: Put every Saturday shift's pay into savings
Ask the union for retraining money for drivers
Discuss moving in with her sister to cut rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd say we've got five years, so no excuses for the government or the company. I'd be pushing for a deal where drivers get first pick of any new jobs at the depot, like supervising the robot fleet. I'd say it at work and at the union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years plus three for the robots is eight, which is longer than I've been driving. That gives me time, but I know myself, I'd waste the first couple of years hoping it isn't real. The bit that scares me is being thirty-five and starting again with nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and put money aside steadily, a hundred a month into a separate account Jo can't see me raid. I'd sign up for whatever the union gets us, maybe a course in fleet supervision or warehouse safety. I'd ask the depot manager straight out which jobs they think will still be there in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but slower worried. There's room to breathe, though I'd still lie awake some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first couple of years. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone setting me a date, honestly, like a union course that starts in March and I've signed up. I don't do well with open-ended. If it's on the calendar I'll turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the depot manager to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want him to say there's a place for the best drivers in whatever comes next. I don't think he'd know, and I don't think he'd tell me if he did. But I'd ask anyway, in front of the others.

say: Five years means **no excuses** for the government or the company.
Drivers should get **first pick** of new depot jobs, like robot fleet supervision.
think: Five years plus three for robots gives me **eight years**, more than I've driven.
I fear being **thirty-five** and starting again with nothing saved.
do: Put **a hundred a month** into a separate savings account.
Sign up for a union **fleet supervision** or warehouse safety course.
Ask the depot manager which jobs will **remain in 2034**.
feel: **Worried** but with room to breathe, still losing some **sleep**.
S3.quote: The bit that scares me is being thirty-five and starting again with nothing saved.
fieldNote: She knows her own habit of **putting things off** and asks for a fixed course date.
The extra years lower the panic but she still expects to **lose the job**, so the mood stays high.
Wants the union to win drivers **first pick** of new roles.

steps.text: Move a hundred a month into a separate savings account
Sign up for a union fleet supervision course starting in March
Ask the depot manager in front of others which jobs remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd say this is a planning problem and the government has no excuse not to plan. I'd want free retraining for every driver and a proper wage floor. I'd say it at the union and probably bore everyone at the pub with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years plus three is 2039, and I'd be forty. That's long enough that I could still drive most of my working life and change once. I'd be less frightened, but I'd still feel like I'm waiting for an eviction notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do almost nothing different, I'll be honest, except stay in the union and keep driving. I'd try to get one month saved, which I've never managed. Maybe in a few years I'd look at the bus licence, because passengers might want a person a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. Ten years is a long time to dread something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is doing almost nothing in the first year a choice or a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I don't like change and I'm not going to pretend I'll suddenly love courses. But it's also that I can't afford a course and the rent at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the bus licence real rather than a maybe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the union or the council paid for it and I could do it on my rest days. Jo would push me, Jo always does. I'd probably start around year five if nothing else had moved.

say: Ten years makes this a **planning problem**, and the government has no excuse.
Every driver should get **free retraining** and a proper wage floor.
think: Robots by **2039** means I could drive most of my career and change once.
It still feels like waiting for an **eviction notice**.
do: Keep driving and stay active in the **union** in the first year.
Try to save **one month** of expenses for the first time.
Consider a **bus licence** around year five if it's paid for.
feel: More **uneasy** than scared, with a long stretch of **dread**.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time to dread something.
fieldNote: The decade lets her **delay action**, which suits her dislike of change.
Money, not willingness alone, blocks retraining: she **can't afford** a course and rent together.
Her partner is the one who **pushes her** to move.

steps.text: Keep driving the chilled supermarket routes from the depot
Save one month of expenses for the first time
Wait until year five before looking at a bus licence

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because I wouldn't have time to save and I wouldn't have time to get over myself and learn something. What would help is the union winning a guaranteed wage while people retrain, paid by the companies that save money on drivers. Without that, Jo and I are on my sister's sofa.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women drivers. There's three of us at the depot and it took me years to be taken seriously. I'd hate to finally be the one they send the new lads to, and then lose it all to a machine.

headlineQuote: I'd hate to finally be the one they send the new lads to, and then lose it all to a machine.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old** fridge truck driver who trains new drivers but stays on the **lower rate**.
She and her partner, a care worker, live with **under a month** of savings above a takeaway.
She avoids apps and change, and leans on the **union** rather than retraining.
She moves from **uneasy** about money in AI Plateau to **alarmed** under fast AGI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to save or to make herself learn something new.
whatWouldHelp: A union-won **guaranteed wage** while retraining, paid by firms that save on drivers.
